newsitem.title: UK: London industrial metals market looks to future.
newsitem.headline: London industrial metals market looks to future.

text.p: The annual gathering of the world's movers and shakers in the metals industry ends on Friday, with a confident LME setting out ideas for the future.
The London Metal Exchange (LME), the world's leading industrial metals market, has been battered by criticism since June when the Sumitomo Corp copper scandal erupted.
But on Tuesday, LME Chairman Raj Bagri made a robust speech at the centrepiece of Metals Week -- the annual LME dinner.
"I think the view was it was time for the LME to take a stand, and hit back to some extent," a leading trader said.

In June, Japan's Sumitomo stunned the metals world by reporting $1.8 billion of losses, subsequently revised up to $2.6 billion, run up in 10 years of alleged unauthorised dealing by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
Bagri not only stoutly defended the market's role in its actions surrounding the Sumitomo affair, he put down a wish-list of potential changes.
"He took the opportunity to defend the LME, and it needed to be said as this was the worst ever thing to hit copper, which is after all the flagship contract," another senior trader said.
Industry sources said that the LME had in effect drawn a line in the sand this week, and stopped backpedalling after months of widespread criticism.

The market was flexible on some changes it might have to make, post-Sumitomo. But there were practices unique to the LME, such as non-cash clearing, that while not exactly cast-in-stone were there to be retained.
"For industry, cash-clearing would be detrimental in terms of cash flow and would fundamentally alter commercial structures within the industry," Bagri said on Tuesday.
Unlike all other futures markets, profits and losses on the LME are not realised until positions mature.

The LME has been forced to address issues such as this as well as over-the-counter (OTC), or off-exchange, trading, transparancy, off-market non-member traders and its whole membership structure by the cataclysm in copper.

Sumitomo said their losses were sustained largely on the LME, which asked Britain's top financial regulator the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) to conduct a wide-ranging review of the market. Consultative papers have been sent out to the industry, with the SIB due to report by the end of the year.
Some veteran traders, with years of experience and long memories, pointed out that the tin market crisis of 1985 resulted in the LME making radical changes.
Eleven year ago metals markets were shaken by an 800,000 million stg default by the International Tin Council as their attempt to support the world tin price failed.

"That was needed at the time, and the LME was able to move forward, while remaining what it started out to be -- a trade market," one said."This (the Sumitomo-affair) undoubtedly hurts, but it gives us another chance to change. Bagri said the LME had been hampered in investigating copper over the years by its inability to prise out information in the OTC and cash markets.

More transparancy and regulation in this murky market is needed, as is control over big players who are not LME members, and changes at the LME itself, industry sources said this week. Bagri said that the LME is reviewing the management and structure of the Board, and this was touched on by Jean-Pierre Rodier, Chairman of France's Pechiney -- the world's fourth biggest aluminium producer. Addressing the LME dinner on Tuesday Rodier called for a better balance on the LME Board in terms of composition and influence. "All activities relating to the metals should be represented," Rodier said.
And another notable change called for by Bagri would be requiring off-market traders become LME members.

"I think that would be spot on. For years these people, who are not just clients but big players, have been feeding off the LME and it is not just in copper. It is about time we got some sort of control," a director at an LME ring-dealer said.
